title: The Bridge and the Novel: What Humanities Departments Never Told You About Yourself
author: Greg O'Keefe
summary: Greg O'Keefe argues that literary analysis and engineering are cognitively isomorphic — that they run the same underlying process (what he calls the decomposition-connection-extension loop) on different substrates, and that humanities graduates leave university equipped with this generalizable analytical architecture but without the vocabulary to claim it. He shows that the standard account of AI's relevance to humanities graduates (the interface changed to natural language, therefore they qualify) understates the structural point: AI has not granted access to a new conversation but revealed what humanities training was always building. By collapsing the distance between intent and implementation, AI has shifted the bottleneck in knowledge work upstream — to problem characterization, decomposition, and synthesis — precisely where humanities graduates were trained to operate. O'Keefe identifies three specific transferable qualities: comfort with ambiguity, facility with shifting abstraction levels, and tolerance for complexity that does not simplify. His institutional diagnosis is that humanities departments undermined themselves by insisting on irreducibility — by claiming they were not like engineering — and in doing so severed the one argument that would have preserved their relevance. The conclusion is not a call to abandon the canon but to change how the chair answers the question: the graduates are already equipped, they just leave without the language to say so.
points: The 'decomposition-connection-extension loop' — encountering a complex object, breaking it into load-bearing components, tracing their relationships, and producing a defensible claim — is identical in literary analysis and engineering; only the validation environment (interpretive community vs. physical reality) differs.

AI has shifted the bottleneck in a growing class of knowledge-work problems from technical execution (which AI now handles) upstream to problem formulation, decomposition, and synthesis — exactly the work humanities training was always developing, even if it never articulated this.

Humanities departments institutionally destroyed their own argument for relevance by insisting on irreducibility ('what we do cannot be formalized, is not like engineering') as a defense against positivism — this protected intrinsic value while severing the extrinsic argument that would have saved enrollment.

The three transferable qualities O'Keefe specifies — comfort with ambiguity, facility with shifting abstraction levels, and tolerance for complexity that does not simplify — are not 'soft skills' but the hard cognitive ceiling on knowledge work in the AI era.

The rebranding he calls for is not a betrayal of humanistic value: keep Middlemarch, keep the esoteric seminar; just change how the chair answers the question 'what are you actually teaching my student to do?' — the answer already available, accurately describing what literary analysis IS.
quotes: You are teaching your student to take a text they have never seen before, decompose it into its constituent components, understand how those components interact under pressure, identify where the argument or the narrative is doing its most important work, propose an interpretation, and defend that interpretation against competing readings. The domain is literature. The method is theirs forever.

The claim I want to make explicit is this: literary analysis and engineering are not two different kinds of thinking applied to different problems. They are the same underlying cognitive process — what we might call the decomposition-connection-extension loop — applied to different substrates.

What AI does, structurally, is collapse the distance between intent and implementation. The bottleneck in a growing class of problems is no longer execution — writing the code, querying the database, building the pipeline. These tasks are increasingly handled at the AI layer. The bottleneck shifts upstream, to the work that precedes execution: correctly characterizing the problem, decomposing it into its components, understanding the relationships that matter, anticipating second-order consequences, and producing a coherent claim about what should be built and why.

Comfort with ambiguity. Literary training insists that you sit with a text that does not resolve cleanly, that resists your first interpretation, that contains genuine tension between competing readings. You are not rewarded for forcing premature closure. You are rewarded for holding the ambiguity long enough to say something true about it. This is exactly the disposition required when working on problems where the parameters are unstable and the requirements are incompletely specified — which describes most real organizational problems.

The humanities defended their value through the 20th century by insisting on irreducibility — on the claim that what they do cannot be formalized, cannot be systematized, is not like engineering or science, belongs to the untranslatable human dimension of experience. The unintended consequence was catastrophic: by insisting they were not like engineering, the humanities severed the one argument that would have preserved their institutional relevance.
AI did not make humanities graduates relevant by changing the interface. It revealed what they were always trained to do by removing the layer of technical execution that had previously obscured it.
The graduates are already equipped. They leave without the language to claim what they carry. The English chair just never told them that.
